transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SRE), Samir Rao (Redwood Perf), Jordan Park (Quantify Labs ML Eng), Maya Patel (Quantify Platform), Evan Rhodes (Quantify CTO), Lena Ortiz (Quantify Infra)

Summary (auto): Deep technical profiling session to compare TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM execution characteristics on Quantify's target hardware (8x A100), focus on kernel selection, CUDA Graphs capture, KV cache behavior with long context, batching strategies, and quantization tradeoffs. Discussed on-prem/VPC deployment constraints and next steps for POC and benchmark artifacts.

Topics: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM tuning, vLLM performance differences, CUDA Graphs usage and pitfalls, KV cache validity & eviction, batching policies, int8/4-bit quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem deployment considerations, POC setup.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alyssa Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a deep dive into the GPU runtime profiling, um mostly focusing on the kernel selection stuff and the tnt-rt— Tenser? uh TensorRT-LLM pathways versus vLLM. Diego will lead the perf captures.
[00:22] Jordan Park: thanks, Alyssa. excited. quick note, we've been seeing weird tail-latency on our 8xA100 jobs when sequence lengths go beyond 2k, so curious if kv cache or batching is blowing up.
[00:35] Diego Morales: cool, that's exactly what we want to look at. quick agenda: 1) show CUDA Graphs capture we did on a 16k context run, 2) point out kernel selection differences between TRT-LLM and vLLM, 3) batching + kv-cache behavior, 4) quantization notes, 5) Q&A + next steps. sound good?
[00:50] Maya Patel: yep. also want to confirm VPC/on-prem constraints — we need no egress and KMS integration.
[00:55] Priya Singh: we'll cover the VPC checklist at the end, short.
[01:05] Samir Rao: jumping in — one quick caveat: our captures are on CUDA 12.3 + cuBLASLt changes, and TensorRT-LLM used TRT 8.6 in our run. small mismatch can change kernel choices.
[01:20] Evan Rhodes: noted, we run 12.2 on prem but can test 12.3 if it's required.

[05:12] Diego Morales: OK, first slide — here's the CUDA Graphs capture. (link: drive.redwood/quantify/cudagraphs-2025-10-28). we instrumented at the kernel level using nvtx ranges so you can see the timeline. major point: TensorRT-LLM produces more fused attention kernels per step, whereas vLLM/transformer stack tends to have more smaller GEMM kernels plus attention parts split out.
[05:40] Jordan Park: when you say fused attention, is that the custom QKV+softmax+matmul fused kernel?
[05:45] Diego Morales: yes, it's the fused QKV-attention kernel in TRT-LLM that reduces kernel launch overhead and host-device syncs. that shows up as a big monolithic kernel block in the graph. vLLM shows more granular launches.
[06:10] Maya Patel: but I'm guessing fused kernels have higher memory pressure? we've seen OOMs on long contexts.
[06:18] Samir Rao: good point — fused kernels often materialize larger intermediate buffers, especially with rotary embeddings and long sequence lengths. we saw a ~10% memory bump in TRT fused path at 16k vs vLLM path because of pre-allocations for the fused attention. sometimes that triggers caching behavior and earlier evictions of KV cache.
[06:42] Jordan Park: that resonates. our memory graph shows eviction around step ~400 on 16k runs.

[08:05] Diego Morales: moving on — kernel selection differences: TRT-LLM picks specialized kernels for attention and has heuristics to choose different GEMM algorithms based on sequence length and batch. vLLM relies on cuBLAS/cuBLASLt heuristics and sometimes uses smaller kernels with tiling that favor throughput at moderate seq lengths.
[08:38] Diego Morales: note: the kernel chooser will swap to int8-friendly kernels if you enable quantization, and that changes runtimes significantly. switching to int8 or 4-bit quant can make latency per token lower but may increase variance if you hit saturation on tensor cores.
[09:02] Jordan Park: what's your recommendation for quantization on long context vs short?
[09:08] Samir Rao: for long contexts we recommend mixed precision (fp16) with selective quantization on MLP layers first. 4-bit on attention tends to produce variable quality/time tradeoffs. also watch for per-channel scales — we use asymmetric scales for some weights to reduce outliers.

[10:30] Maya Patel: Diego, can you show the actual CUDA Graph timeline and mark the KV cache loads?
[10:36] Diego Morales: yes — here's the annotated timeline. (shared). you can see the KV loads as periodic smaller memcpy kernels followed by attention kernels that consume them. in TRT-LLM, the KV loads are batched into fewer larger memcpy calls, vLLM often has more frequent smaller memcpy/kcopy ops.
[11:00] Jordan Park: that smaller-more-frequent pattern probably explains our higher PCIe overhead. we use NVLink but still see inter-socket transfers when shards move.
[11:12] Lena Ortiz: we are sharding KV across GPUs to save memory; if TRT fuses and wants contiguous KV that might force a different layout?
[11:20] Diego Morales: exactly; layout mismatch is common. TRT-LLM may prefer interleaved contiguous KV, vLLM uses per-shard KV buffers. so one solution is to normalize the KV layout at load time, but that has a cost. in our POC we implemented a fast re-layout kernel that runs once per window.

[14:42] Diego Morales: batching: we ran micro-batching experiments. continuous batching with short latency SLOs tends to benefit from vLLM's scheduler because it's more flexible about merging variable-length requests. TRT-LLM with static batching can hit better peak throughput but suffers when there is tail-latency due to jumbo requests.
[15:05] Samir Rao: example numbers from our run: on 8xA100, 8-token context steady-state, TRT-LLM achieved 9.6 tokens/s per GPU (FP16 fused kernels) vs vLLM ~8.9 tokens/s. at 2048 tokens context with KV warm, vLLM had better tail-latency because its per-step kernel latency was smaller and more consistent.
[15:40] Jordan Park: interesting — so TRT is better in small context steady state, vLLM better for long contexts and more variable sizes.
[15:48] Diego Morales: yeah; and the crossover depends on model size, KV cache hit ratio, and batching policy. we gave you a spreadsheet (link: drive.redwood/quantify/benchmark-workbook) with sensitivity tables.

[18:00] Maya Patel: can you explain the CUDA Graph pitfalls you mentioned earlier? like replay/graph capture invalidation? we've tried to capture graphs but sometimes they re-record mid-run.
[18:10] Priya Singh: short version: CUDA Graphs are great to reduce launch overhead, but any change in shapes, allocation pointers, or kernel selection can cause capture invalidation. for example, if TRT chooses a different kernel algorithm mid-run (due to a different sequence length or a different cached algo), the graph must be re-captured. that re-capture causes a blocking operation.
[18:36] Diego Morales: we often keep two captures: one for short-context flows and one for long-context flows, and switch at a boundary with minimal overlap. that reduces re-capture frequency. also pin memory and pre-allocate KV buffers to keep pointers stable.
[19:00] Jordan Park: that's useful — we saw re-captures correlate with spikes.

[21:55] Diego Morales: quantization notes quickly: 8-bit dynamic quant yields safe perf wins with minimal quality loss for most MLPs. 4-bit requires calibration and per-channel scaling; also watch for fused kernels that assume fp16 and break or degrade when weight layout changes. TRT-LLM has specialized 4-bit kernels but they're sometimes brittle across model variants. vLLM + custom quant path can be more conservative but stable.
[22:30] Samir Rao: don't forget evaluation: we recommend running downstream quality evals (the evals deck) before rolling quantization into production. small perplexity increases can hide regressions.

[25:10] Maya Patel: VPC/on-prem notes: we need to ensure KMS/HSM integration and no external telemetry. what's Redwood's typical private deployment for this?
[25:20] Priya Singh: Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC — control plane minimal egress, optional on-prem agent for air-gapped, KMS integration supported (we have docs). we'll send the checklist. key items: storage encryption at rest, network egress rules, audit log forwarding, and HSM/KMS config.
[25:45] Evan Rhodes: great. we will need SOC2 artefacts and audit logs retention policy — can you include that?
[25:52] Priya Singh: yes, we'll include SOC2 summary and retention options.

[28:00] Jordan Park: one practical question: our architecture uses sharded model weights across GPUs for memory. TRT-LLM expects a contiguous weight layout for some fused kernels. how disruptive is layout normalization?
[28:15] Diego Morales: it depends — for many models we can use a lazy re-layout at startup or a small conversion pass. cost is a one-time copy plus some CPU/GPU time; we measured ~45s on a 8xA100 to convert an LLaMA-derivative weights set into contiguous fused layout. that may be acceptable during deployment initialization.
[28:40] Lena Ortiz: 45s is fine. but we need idempotent startup for canary and A/B.

[31:05] Diego Morales: another runtime trick: KV cache eviction. if memory pressure spikes, some runtimes evict older KV entries which causes recompute and large latency spikes. we instrumented eviction points in the CUDA Graph and correlated them to host-side GC triggers. recommendation: set a reserve buffer for KV cache to avoid eviction under bursty loads.
[31:34] Samir Rao: also watch the GPU allocator — default caching allocators can unpredictably grow. pinning and using our recommended allocator config reduces fragmentation. we'll share the allocator knobs in the workbook.

[34:50] Jordan Park: on the bench data: are there per-layer hotspots we should focus on for kernel selection?
[34:55] Samir Rao: attention and the first MLP matmuls (pre-MLP projection) are the biggest hotspots. fused attention reduces host->device syncs but increases kernel complexity. sometimes switching attention to a different algorithm (e.g., flash attention variant) improves tail. we tested a patch where TRT used a different attention kernel for seq>1024 and saw ~12% reduced tail latency.

[38:10] Maya Patel: do you have a recommended default config for POC? like batch size, max merge window, kv reserve?
[38:20] Diego Morales: yes — recommended starting config (we put in the workbook): max_batch_merge_window_ms=40, max_batch_size=64, kv_reserve_ratio=0.15, preallocate_kv=True, use_fp16, enable_int8_for_mlp=false (turn on after eval). these are conservative and avoid evictions.
[38:45] Jordan Park: good, we'll try that.

[42:00] Priya Singh: security note — for on-prem we recommend using your KMS with envelope encryption and Redwood's private mode which runs the control plane in your VPC. logs can forward to your SIEM. no telemetry required.

[45:12] Diego Morales: demo: I want to show the capture where we annotated kernel times. (screen). you can see repeated patterns per autoregressive step: memcpy(KV load) -> fused-attn kernel -> MLP kernels -> memcpy(out). the important part is where we see a different GEMM algo in the middle of the run — that forced re-capture.
[45:45] Jordan Park: is that algo change due to cuBLASLt heuristics or due to shape changes?
[45:50] Diego Morales: both. cuBLASLt may pick a different algo when it thinks another is better for current shapes; shape changes (context length) also trigger heuristics. locking to a specific algo is possible but can be risky across hardware.

[49:00] Maya Patel: any tips to force deterministic kernel selection?
[49:05] Samir Rao: we sometimes set cublasLt front-end preferences and set algorithm overrides, but test across your matrix. also force deterministic seeds for autotuning. there is a tradeoff: you may lose perf in some cases but gain stability for CUDA Graph capture.

[52:20] Evan Rhodes: on the POC — what should we measure and what artifacts do you want from our side?
[52:28] Diego Morales: please collect: nvprof/nvtx captures, nvlink/pci metrics, GPU utilization, allocator stats, and full logs of kernel launches if possible. we gave a script in the workbook. also include traffic profile (request sizes, seq length distribution).

[55:10] Jordan Park: small thing — we have a mixed cluster with M60s for other workloads. is there any gotcha when mixing older GPUs with A100s for model serving?
[55:20] Samir Rao: don't mix during a single model replica. mixing is ok at cluster level but avoid scheduling shards of the same replica across generations; kernel choices and tensor core availability differ a lot.

[58:40] Diego Morales: wrapping up — we'll upload the annotated graphs, the workbook, and recommended config. we'll also send the private deployment checklist and SOC2 summary.
[59:02] Alyssa Chen: recap on next steps: Diego uploads captures and workbook, Priya sends VPC checklist & SOC2 summary, Jordan runs baseline tests and returns logs, schedule follow-up week of Nov 10.
[59:20] Jordan Park: sounds good. thanks, everyone.

[60:00] Maya Patel: quick question — any blockers on Redwood side for on-prem?
[60:06] Priya Singh: no blockers; we do require a short security review and access to your KMS details to configure envelope keys — policy review shouldn't take more than a week.

[62:00] Alyssa Chen: great. final notes: we'll attach the benchmark workbook with sensitivity tables and the POC runbook. Diego — can you add a small how-to for capturing CUDA Graphs in that workbook?
[62:10] Diego Morales: yes, already drafting a step-by-step. includes NVTX tagging, pinning, where to look for re-captures.

[66:00] Evan Rhodes: thanks everyone — appreciate the depth.
[66:05] Alyssa Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up in email with links and scheduling.

End of recording.

References shared: drive.redwood/quantify/cudagraphs-2025-10-28, drive.redwood/quantify/benchmark-workbook, redwood.com/docs/private-deployments-vpc-checklist.pdf
